Kenya Airways is looking to strengthen its Nigerian operations amid rising competition and growing demand for air travel. Country Manager, Nigeria, James Nganga, speaks with ODINAKA ANUDU on the airline’s strategy, growth plans, competition and challenges in Nigeria’s aviation market Nigeria has been one of Kenya Airways’ longest-serving markets in recent times. How much has passenger traffic on the Lagos-Nairobi route grown over the past three years, and what growth target have you set for 2027? Nigeria is very important to Kenya Airways and is one of the most strategic markets we operate in Africa, if not the world. The Lagos-Nairobi route has recorded significant growth and demonstrated resilience, particularly following the COVID-19 pandemic. I would rather not disclose specific figures because I do not want to give competitors visibility into what we are doing. However, if I recall correctly, we had a target of about 70,000 passengers for 2025, representing tickets sold in Nigeria, and we met and surpassed that target. For 2026, we were given a growth target of 25 per cent, reflecting steady growth and increasing demand from the Nigerian market. Our passenger traffic comprises business travellers, students, particularly those studying in Kenya, and passengers travelling within Africa. For 2027, I believe our target is close to 100,000 passengers, representing growth of approximately 25 to 30 per cent compared with the previous year. In your recent statement, I noticed that Kenya Airways is increasingly targeting millennials and Generation Z travellers in Nigeria. What opportunities do you see in these demographics, and what proportion of your Nigerian passenger base currently falls within these groups? Millennials and Generation Z represent one of the fastest-growing travel segments, not just in Nigeria but globally. This demographic is highly mobile, digitally connected and adventurous. They are particularly interested in adventure travel, experiential travel and education. I recently attended a TechCabal event, and I was amazed by the number of young people, particularly millennials and Gen Zs, in attendance. I was sharing with my team how young and energetic the participants were. We are seeing this trend replicated across Africa. Young people are adventurous and interested in sports and education. I also met several young founders and chief executives at the conference who were intelligent and ambitious. This presents opportunities not only in Nigeria but across Africa and the global market. They account for a significant proportion of our customer database, and we recognise their influence on travel trends. To reach them, we engage with them through various digital platforms. We have introduced technology into our mobile booking channels and offer flexible travel options through periodic campaigns and promotional fares. We also receive partnership requests from organisations hosting conferences and events targeted at this demographic. Where possible, we participate by offering sponsorships, including complimentary tickets or discounts to eligible conference participants. These are some of the ways we engage with this growing market. Given that this demographic is largely technology-savvy and digitally connected, how is Kenya Airways adopting technology across its services and operations It depends on the different customer touchpoints, including booking channels, the travel experience and the check-in process. The company has invested significantly in its digital platforms and website, as well as in operational technology. We have also recorded improvements in our in-flight entertainment systems. We are ensuring that aircraft being introduced into our fleet are equipped with in-flight entertainment systems. At the airport, we recognise that the traditional check-in process, which requires passengers to queue, can be improved. Airports have introduced check-in kiosks, but airlines must also ensure that their systems are sufficiently advanced to integrate with these facilities. We also try to reach younger travellers through social media platforms such as TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Our head office has a dedicated team responsible for managing these engagements and communicating with customers across the platforms. Beyond that, we recognise that tourism and air travel are significant industries with opportunities for technology entrepreneurs. For people interested in entering the travel business, we offer New Distribution Capability, through which the airline makes its inventory available to third parties. This creates opportunities for young entrepreneurs to operate as intermediaries and facilitate ticket purchases for customers. We therefore make our inventory available through these distribution channels. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Which routes are recording the strongest connecting traffic from Nigeria, and what opportunities do you see in expanding this transit business? First, I would like to comment on the growth in traffic to Nairobi. Following the removal of visa requirements for citizens of 52 African countries, including Nigeria, passenger numbers have increased by almost 45 per cent year to date compared with the corresponding period last year. That figure relates specifically to passengers travelling to Nairobi. However, Nairobi traffic alone is not sufficient to fill an entire aircraft, which is why we connect passengers to other important destinations. Outside Nairobi, some of our major connecting destinations include London and JFK in New York. Towards the East, we connect passengers to China, particularly Guangzhou, as well as Dubai and India. Within Africa, we record significant passenger traffic to East African countries, especially Rwanda and Uganda, as well as Johannesburg in South Africa. Holidaymakers also travel to destinations such as Mauritius and Sicily. Our strategy is to ensure that our flights provide convenient connections to these destinations. Since we operate daily flights into Lagos, we try to provide passengers with several onward travel options, with some destinations served four or five times a week. Our head office and network planning teams consider the Nigerian market when planning flight schedules because passengers from Nigeria contribute to the success of these routes. Ultimately, the success of a destination depends on the number of passengers an airline can attract. We therefore ensure that connections from Lagos through Nairobi are as seamless as possible by reducing waiting times. Ideally, we try to keep connecting times between two and three hours in Nairobi, although some connections are shorter, ranging from one hour to about one hour and 30 minutes. The objective is to provide convenient connections that encourage more passengers to travel through Nairobi to other destinations. The Nigerian aviation market is highly competitive, with several airlines operating in the market. How does Kenya Airways compete, particularly on the Lagos-Nairobi route, and what differentiates its services? Competition has increased significantly, with airlines expanding their frequencies and increasing the number of flights they operate. In such an environment, airlines must remain competitive because customers have several options. Even if an airline wants to charge a particular fare, passengers may choose another carrier if better alternatives are available. One of our strategies is to offer early-bird promotions. Although airlines generally operate under similar pricing principles, we encourage passengers to change their booking habits by purchasing tickets early to access better fares. We also introduce special seasonal offers and tactical campaigns. Depending on the season, we communicate promotional offers to customers, sometimes offering discounts of 20 to 30 per cent. At the same time, we remain conscious of operating costs, including fuel expenses, which may differ among airlines depending on their respective markets and supply arrangements. We also respond to changing market conditions through promotional fares and tactical campaigns. At the moment, for instance, passengers are looking out for Black Friday and other promotional offers. Another strategy is working with travel agents. Some customers have established relationships with particular agents and may enjoy credit facilities through them. We therefore make our inventory and promotional messages accessible through travel agents to give customers greater flexibility. Airfares are also reviewed continuously. When global fuel prices increased around March and April, many airlines adjusted their fares. However, whenever there is some relief in operating costs, we also make corresponding adjustments. Pricing is influenced by market conditions and internal considerations, including taxes in the different countries where we operate. One of the challenges facing Nigerian consumers is declining purchasing power, particularly following the depreciation of the naira. How affordable are Kenya Airways’ fares for Nigerian travellers, and what are you doing to ensure they remain accessible? I believe our fares are competitive and affordable because we operate in a highly competitive market. An airline may want to charge exorbitant fares, but the Nigerian market has a way of communicating its position. Customers will simply choose not to fly with you. If you see us recording increasing demand, expanding seat capacity and carrying more passengers, it indicates that our fares are competitive. Most airlines follow similar pricing principles, which are driven by demand and supply across different seasons. During high-demand periods, particularly when flight loads are high, fares tend to increase. For example, flights to Europe have different low-season and high-season fares. We respond to these market conditions accordingly. We also conduct regular fare-monitoring exercises, usually every other week, to assess what competitors are offering and guide our pricing decisions. Depending on the market situation and the demand we are trying to stimulate, we introduce tactical and promotional fares when we notice that demand is under pressure. How important is the Nigerian market to Kenya Airways, and what proportion of your international passenger business is generated from Nigeria? Nigeria is extremely important to us. I usually tell people that if you are not flying to Nigeria, you are not doing business. The importance of the market is demonstrated by the fact that Nigeria was among the stations we relaunched after the COVID-19 pandemic. Although I was not here at the time, I understand that Nigeria was one of the markets that quickly returned to daily flights. We initially resumed operations with three flights, but within approximately two months, we had returned to daily services. That demonstrates how important the Nigerian market is to the organisation. The passengers we carry from Nigeria generate significant revenue for the airline. It is also important to understand that the traffic is not limited to passengers travelling between Lagos and Nairobi. Nigerian passengers also connect through Nairobi to destinations such as London, Dubai and New York, particularly JFK. Therefore, Nigeria contributes to our connecting passenger traffic as well as cargo opportunities. We have corporate agreements with multinational companies and small and medium-sized enterprises that need to travel for business, source goods or provide services. We also have partnerships with travel agencies. I believe we have more than 3,000 IATA-accredited agents who help distribute our inventory and seats in the Nigerian market. Beyond this, there are opportunities associated with our international workforce, tourism and sports, particularly football. Nigeria’s large population and vibrant business environment are also contributing to the growth of its middle-class travelling population, which is an important market for us. Overall, Nigeria is extremely important to Kenya Airways. Beyond the positive aspects of operating in Nigeria, what challenges has Kenya Airways encountered in the market, and what is the airline doing to address them? One of the major challenges facing the aviation industry since the COVID-19 pandemic has been the shortage of aircraft spare parts and aircraft themselves. As a result, we do not currently have sufficient capacity. Although we operate daily flights into Nigeria, we would like to increase our frequencies. However, we are constrained by the number of aircraft available to us. This affects the level of service we would ideally like to provide. Some of our passengers, particularly traders travelling to Dubai, have raised concerns about baggage capacity. For instance, instead of deploying our larger Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft, we sometimes operate the Boeing 737. This limits the amount of baggage we can accommodate for traders. Aircraft availability is therefore one of our biggest challenges. However, the leadership at our head office has reassured us that efforts are being made to acquire more aircraft, including through leasing arrangements and efforts to accelerate existing orders from Boeing. Another challenge relates to the in-flight entertainment experience. As part of our efforts to improve customer experience, we have been phasing out older aircraft that do not have in-flight entertainment systems. I believe we currently have only one aircraft remaining without the facility. We are also looking at introducing internet connectivity on board, but this requires significant investment. Passengers have told us that they want internet access during flights. Our leadership is aware of this feedback and is working towards making it available. Some airlines, including Emirates, already offer internet connectivity on their flights. What is preventing Kenya Airways from providing the same service? Again, it comes down to money and prioritisation. Although we want to improve the customer experience, we must consider where our available resources will have the greatest impact. We could invest in providing internet connectivity, but those resources could also be used to acquire another aircraft, which is currently a more pressing need for us. As much as we want to improve the passenger experience, we must also prioritise our core product, which is transportation. At the moment, both the airline and our passengers recognise that the immediate priority is to ensure that people can travel and connect to more destinations. Achieving that requires additional aircraft. We will get there, but for now, acquiring more aircraft is our most pressing need and requires a significant proportion of our resources. Odinaka Anudu
